claim: GAPs were formed by an acetylcholine (ACh)-dependent endocytic event that delivers fluid-phase cargo retrograde into the trans-golgi network and across the cell by transcytosis.
source: Using high-resolution light and electron microscopy, we found that in mice, GAPs were formed by an acetylcholine (ACh)-dependent endocytic event remarkable for delivery of fluid-phase cargo retrograde into the trans-golgi network and across the cell by transcytosis – in addition to the expected transport of fluid-phase cargo by endosomes to multi-vesicular bodies and lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from high-resolution light and electron microscopy studies in mice.

claim: GAPs transport fluid-phase cargo by endosomes to multi-vesicular bodies and lysosomes.
source: Using high-resolution light and electron microscopy, we found that in mice, GAPs were formed by an acetylcholine (ACh)-dependent endocytic event remarkable for delivery of fluid-phase cargo retrograde into the trans-golgi network and across the cell by transcytosis – in addition to the expected transport of fluid-phase cargo by endosomes to multi-vesicular bodies and lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from high-resolution light and electron microscopy studies in mice.

claim: ACh-induced GAP formation and mucin secretion are functionally independent.
source: While ACh also induced goblet cells to secrete mucins, ACh-induced GAP formation and mucin secretion were functionally independent and mediated by different receptors and signaling pathways, enabling goblet cells to differentially regulate these processes to accommodate the dynamically changing demands of the mucosal environment for barrier maintenance and sampling of lumenal substances.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that ACh-induced GAP formation and mucin secretion are mediated by different receptors and signaling pathways.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that different receptors and signaling pathways mediate these processes.

claim: Goblet cells can differentially regulate GAP formation and mucin secretion to accommodate the dynamically changing demands of the mucosal environment.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings that GAP formation and mucin secretion are functionally independent and mediated by different pathways.

claim: The gastrointestinal immune system samples gut lumenal contents to induce adaptive immune responses characterized by T cell-mediated antigen-specific tolerance.
source: It has long been appreciated that the gastrointestinal immune system is not ignorant of the lumenal contents, and in the healthy state gut lumenal contents are sampled to induce adaptive immune responses, characterized by T cell-mediated antigen-specific tolerance.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific consensus about gastrointestinal immune system function.

claim: Goblet cells have a well-established role in innate immunity through secretion of mucins and maintenance of the mucus layer.
source: Goblet cells (GCs) are specialized intestinal epithelial cells that have a well-established role in innate immunity through secretion of mucins and maintenance of the mucus layer.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about goblet cell function.

claim: The mucus layer provides a first line of defense against physical and chemical injury and protects against pathogen invasion.
source: The mucus layer provides a first line of defense against physical and chemical injury and protects against pathogen invasion (Kim and Ho, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim and Ho, 2010.

claim: Goblet cells produce and secrete biologically active products that contribute to innate immunity by promoting epithelial restitution, inhibiting intestinal nematode chemotaxis, and stabilizing the mucus layer.
source: GCs also produce and secrete biologically active products that contribute to innate immunity by promoting epithelial restitution, inhibiting intestinal nematode chemotaxis, and stabilizing the mucus layer (Herbert et al., 2009; Johansson et al., 2009; Taupin and Podolsky, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Herbert et al., 2009; Johansson et al., 2009; Taupin and Podolsky, 2003.

claim: Goblet cells can form GC-associated antigen passages (GAPs) which deliver lumenal substances to lamina propria antigen presenting cells to generate antigen-specific T cell responses.
source: Recently, a new role for GCs in intestinal immunity was identified; the ability of GCs to form GC-associated antigen passages (GAPs), which deliver lumenal substances to lamina propria antigen presenting cells to generate antigen-specific T cell responses (Knoop et al., 2017a; Knoop et al., 2017b; Knoop et al., 2015; McDole et al., 2012; Knoop et al., 2017b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Knoop et al., 2017a; Knoop et al., 2017b; Knoop et al., 2015; McDole et al., 2012; Knoop et al., 2017b.

claim: Acetylcholine (ACh) induces GAP formation in the homeostatic state.
source: The potent GC secretagogue acetylcholine (ACh) induces GAP formation in the homeostatic state (Knoop et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014), indicating that GAP formation and mucus secretion can be induced by the same stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Knoop et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014.

claim: GAP formation and mucus secretion can be induced by the same stimulus.
source: The potent GC secretagogue acetylcholine (ACh) induces GAP formation in the homeostatic state (Knoop et al., 2015; Miller et al., 2014), indicating that GAP formation and mucus secretion can be induced by the same stimulus.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that ACh induces both GAP formation and mucus secretion.

claim: GAP formation and the delivery of lumenal substances to the immune compartment are closely regulated to prevent inflammatory responses to gut bacteria and dietary antigens.
source: However, GAP formation and the delivery of lumenal substances to the immune compartment are closely regulated to prevent inflammatory responses to gut bacteria and dietary antigens in settings where the secretion of mucus to maintain the barrier is critical (Knoop et al., 2017a; Knoop et al., 2016; Kulkarni et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Knoop et al., 2017a; Knoop et al., 2016; Kulkarni et al., 2018.

claim: The cytoplasm of GCs forming GAPs is not completely filled with fluorescent luminal cargo.
source: The appearance of SI GAPs by structured illumination microscopy (SIM) revealed that the cytoplasm of GCs forming GAPs was not completely filled with the fluorescent luminal cargo, rather the luminal solute tracer was contained within a network of vesicular appearing structures located predominantly at the periphery of the cell and extending from apical to basolateral cell surfaces, but largely excluded from the region where mucin granules are contained within the theca.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from structured illumination microscopy (SIM) as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Luminal solute tracer in GAPs is contained within a network of vesicular appearing structures located predominantly at the periphery of the cell and extending from apical to basolateral cell surfaces.

claim: GAPs are formed by an active endocytic process that delivers fluid-phase cargo across the epithelial barrier to the lamina propria.
source: The vesicular patterns observed suggested that GAPs were formed by an active endocytic process that delivered fluid-phase cargo across the epithelial barrier to the lamina propria.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the vesicular patterns observed in microscopy data.

claim: Blockade of endocytosis by the dynamin inhibitors Dyngo 4a and dynasore strongly attenuates GAP formation.
source: Indeed, blockade of endocytosis by the dynamin inhibitors Dyngo 4a and dynasore strongly attenuated GAP formation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that dynamin inhibitors reduce GAP formation as shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Inhibition of actin polymerization using cytochalasin D results in a significant reduction in GAP formation.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that cytochalasin D reduces GAP formation as shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: GAPs represent a fluid-phase endocytic pathway capable of delivering lumenal solutes across the cell by transcytosis.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and supported by citations to Clague et al., 1995; Gottlieb et al., 1993; Thyberg and Stenseth, 1981.

claim: Lumenal administration of FM 1-43FX resulted in intracellular staining of a subset of GCs with a staining pattern similar to that of endocytosed dextran.
source: Lumenal administration of FM 1–43FX resulted in intracellular staining of a subset of GCs, with a staining pattern similar to that of endocytosed dextran (Figure 1E compare with Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FM 1-43FX staining as shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1B.

claim: A similar staining pattern of dextran-Alexa647 and FM 1-43FX was observed within the same cell having GC morphology.
source: To evaluate whether endocytosed dextran localized to newly endocytosed membrane structures within the same cell, FM 1–43FX and 10 kDa dextran-Alexa647 were co-administered into the SI lumen and the intracellular staining pattern was evaluated by confocal microscopy. We observed a similar staining pattern of dextran-Alexa647 and FM 1–43FX within the same cell having GC morphology (Figure 1F), further supporting that GAP formation represents an endocytic process.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The pattern and morphology of dextran-containing endosomes in absorptive cells differ from those in GCs.
source: In addition to observing intracellular FM 1–43FX staining and dextran uptake by GCs, we also observed uptake of lumenal dextran by surrounding intestinal epithelial cells. However, the pattern and morphology of dextran-containing endosomes in absorptive cells differed from those in GCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy observations.

claim: In GCs, dextran-containing structures are observed throughout the cell, whereas in adjacent epithelial cells (likely enterocytes), a punctuated pattern of FM 1-43FX staining and dextran uptake is observed localized to the apical cytoplasm.
source: In GCs (asterisk; Figure 1G and upper panel insets), dextran-containing structures were observed throughout the cell, whereas in adjacent epithelial cells, likely enterocytes (arrows; Figure 1G and lower panel insets), a punctuated pattern of FM 1–43FX staining and dextran uptake was observed localized to the apical cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from microscopy as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In adjacent epithelial cells, co-localization of dextran-containing vesicles and the early endosome marker EEA1 was observed.
source: In adjacent epithelial cells, we also observed co-localization of dextran-containing vesicles and the early endosome marker EEA1 (arrows; Figure 1H), but EEA1 staining was not apparent in the endocytic vesicles of adjacent GCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: EEA1 staining was not apparent in the endocytic vesicles of GCs forming GAPs.
source: In adjacent epithelial cells, we also observed co-localization of dextran-containing vesicles and the early endosome marker EEA1 (arrows; Figure 1H), but EEA1 staining was not apparent in the endocytic vesicles of adjacent GCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The vesicles and trafficking pathways of fluid-phase endocytosis differ between GCs forming GAPs and adjacent enterocytes.
source: Thus, the vesicles and trafficking pathways of fluid-phase endocytosis differ between GCs forming GAPs and adjacent enterocytes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations of different staining patterns and endosome markers.

claim: Endocytosed dextran in GAPs was seen in apically located endosomes, multi-vesicular bodies (MVBs), lysosomes, the TGN, and in vesicles close to basolateral membrane consistent with delivery of dextran into the transcytotic pathway.
source: The endocytosed dextran was seen in apically located endosomes, multi-vesicular bodies (MVBs), lysosomes, the TGN, and in vesicles close to basolateral membrane consistent with delivery of dextran into the transcytotic pathway (Figure 2A and B and Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FIB-SEM as shown in Figure 2A and B and Video 2.

claim: Shuttling of endocytosed cargo to endo-lysosomal structures as well as the TGN is consistent with models of fluid-phase endocytosis and their trafficking in most cell types.
source: Shuttling of endocytosed cargo to endo-lysosomal structures as well as the TGN is consistent with models of fluid-phase endocytosis and their trafficking in most cell types (Maxfield and McGraw, 2004), and the specialized need for compensatory endocytosis required by secretory cell types like GCs to recycle large amounts of membrane back into the secretory pathway (i.e., TGN) after exocytosis (Engisch and Nowycky, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maxfield and McGraw, 2004 and Engisch and Nowycky, 1998.

claim: The endocytic vesicles in GCs forming GAPs did not stain positive for EEA1, a marker of early endosomes.
source: Notably the endocytic vesicles in GCs forming GAPs did not stain positive for EEA1 (Figure 1H), a marker of early endosomes, or the late endosome marker Rab7 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but did in some cells stain positive for the lysosome marker LAMP-1 and the TGN marker TGN46 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 1H.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The endocytic vesicles in GCs forming GAPs did in some cells stain positive for the lysosome marker LAMP-1.

claim: In GCs forming GAPs, Rab3D co-localized with areas of dextran uptake.
source: To explore if the endosomes of GAPs could be related to membrane retrieval following secretory granule exocytosis, we examined the location of the secretory granule protein Rab3D that has been shown to be retrieved and redistributed to the TGN following regulated secretion in GCs and pancreatic acinar cells (Jena et al., 1994; Valentijn et al., 2007). We found that in GCs forming GAPs, Rab3D co-localized with areas of dextran uptake, while in GCs not forming GAPs, Rab3D was localized to the secretory granules within the GC theca (Figure 2C and compare with Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In GCs not forming GAPs, Rab3D was localized to the secretory granules within the GC theca.
source: We found that in GCs forming GAPs, Rab3D co-localized with areas of dextran uptake, while in GCs not forming GAPs, Rab3D was localized to the secretory granules within the GC theca (Figure 2C and compare with Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A similar staining pattern was observed when evaluating the localization of the secretory granule protein VAMP8 in GCs forming GAPs.
source: A similar staining pattern was observed when evaluating the localization of the secretory granule protein VAMP8 in GCs forming GAPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GAP endosomes could be related to membrane retrieval following secretory granule exocytosis.
source: These results could be consistent with GAP endosomes forming as a result of membrane recycling after secretory granule exocytosis, which was supported by findings of dextran localizing to wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-positive vesicular structures in GCs forming GAPs (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations of Rab3D and VAMP8 localization and dextran co-localization with WGA.

claim: Dextran localizes to wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-positive vesicular structures in GCs forming GAPs.
source: These results could be consistent with GAP endosomes forming as a result of membrane recycling after secretory granule exocytosis, which was supported by findings of dextran localizing to wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-positive vesicular structures in GCs forming GAPs (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: GCs forming GAPs deliver fluid-phase cargo into the transcytotic pathway, as evidenced by dextran-containing vesicles closely adjacent to the basolateral membranes.
source: Furthermore, unlike absorptive intestinal epithelial cells where transcytosis is largely restricted to receptor-mediated endocytosis (Fung et al., 2018), the GCs forming GAPs appeared to deliver fluid-phase cargo into the transcytotic pathway, as evidenced by dextran-containing vesicles closely adjacent to the basolateral membranes (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FIB-SEM as shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Fung et al., 2018.

claim: Dextran-containing cargo was observed at a fusion point of GCs and adjacent cells in the lamina propria.
source: In some cases, dextran-containing cargo was observed at a fusion point of GCs and adjacent cells in the lamina propria (Figure 2F and G), which is consistent with the transfer of luminal cargo taken up by GAPs to lamina propria MNPs we observed by SIM (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TEM as shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: GAPs represent a fluid-phase transcellular endocytic process capable of efficiently delivering lumenal substances across the epithelial barrier to be captured by phagocytic cells of the innate immune system.
source: These results suggest that GAPs represent a fluid-phase transcellular endocytic process capable of efficiently delivering lumenal substances across the epithelial barrier to be captured by phagocytic cells of the innate immune system.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations of dextran transfer to lamina propria cells.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Knoop et al., 2015; Kulkarni et al., 2020.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Knoop et al., 2015; Kulkarni et al., 2020.

claim: In the SI, steady-state GAP formation is mediated by ACh acting on mAChR4 expressed by GCs.
source: In the SI, steady-state GAP formation is mediated by ACh acting on mAChR4 expressed by GCs (Knoop et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knoop et al., 2015.

claim: ACh is a potent GC secretagogue known to induce secretion of large quantities of mucus by activation of mAChRs when added to intestinal explants.
source: ACh is a potent GC secretagogue known to induce secretion of large quantities of mucus by activation of mAChRs when added to intestinal explants.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about ACh effects on goblet cells.

claim: Baseline mucus secretion in the intestine has not been linked to muscarinic receptor activation.
source: However, baseline mucus secretion in the intestine has not been linked to muscarinic receptor activation (Specian and Neutra, 1980), suggesting that during steady state, activation of mAChR4 triggers endocytic retrieval of secretory granule membrane without being the main driver of secretory granule exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Specian and Neutra, 1980.

claim: During steady state, activation of mAChR4 triggers endocytic retrieval of secretory granule membrane without being the main driver of secretory granule exocytosis.
source: However, baseline mucus secretion in the intestine has not been linked to muscarinic receptor activation (Specian and Neutra, 1980), suggesting that during steady state, activation of mAChR4 triggers endocytic retrieval of secretory granule membrane without being the main driver of secretory granule exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that baseline mucus secretion is not linked to muscarinic receptor activation.

claim: Inhibition of mAChR4 signaling by tropicamide reduced GAP formation in the SI villus and crypt.
source: Our results showed that inhibition of mAChR4 signaling by tropicamide reduced GAP formation in the SI villus and crypt as expected (Figure 3A and B, image E), but had no measurable effect on mucus secretion, quantified as WGA+ mucus area per villus or crypt cross section (Figure 3C and D, image E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data as shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Inhibition of mAChR4 signaling by tropicamide had no measurable effect on mucus secretion in the SI.
source: Our results showed that inhibition of mAChR4 signaling by tropicamide reduced GAP formation in the SI villus and crypt as expected (Figure 3A and B, image E), but had no measurable effect on mucus secretion, quantified as WGA+ mucus area per villus or crypt cross section (Figure 3C and D, image E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data as shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: GAP formation in the distal colon is driven by ACh acting on muscarinic receptors, but independent of mAChR4 signaling.
source: We have previously shown that GAP formation in the distal colon is driven by ACh acting on muscarinic receptors, but independent of mAChR4 signaling (Kulkarni et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kulkarni et al., 2020.

claim: Colonic GCs express mAChR3 and mAChR1.
source: However, colonic GCs have been shown to express mAChR3 and mAChR1 (Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018.

claim: Treatment of mice with 4-DAMP significantly decreased distal colon GAP formation similar to that observed with the pan-muscarinic receptor antagonist atropine.
source: Treatment of mice with 4-DAMP significantly decreased distal colon GAP formation similar to that observed with the pan-muscarinic receptor antagonist atropine, while the mAChR1 antagonist telenzepine had no measurable effect on GAP formation (Figure 3F, image G), indicating that distal colonic GAPs are driven by mAChR3 signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data as shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The mAChR1 antagonist telenzepine had no measurable effect on GAP formation in the distal colon.
source: Treatment of mice with 4-DAMP significantly decreased distal colon GAP formation similar to that observed with the pan-muscarinic receptor antagonist atropine, while the mAChR1 antagonist telenzepine had no measurable effect on GAP formation (Figure 3F, image G), indicating that distal colonic GAPs are driven by mAChR3 signaling.

claim: Distal colonic GAPs are driven by mAChR3 signaling.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations with 4-DAMP and telenzepine.

claim: Inhibition of mAChR3 signaling using 4-DAMP had no measurable effect on mucus secretion in the distal colon.
source: Similar to the SI, inhibition of mAChR3 signaling using 4-DAMP had no measurable effect on mucus secretion in the distal colon as evaluated by Ulex europaeus agglutinin 1 (UEA1+) mucus area per crypt cross section (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data as shown in Figure 3H.

claim: mAChR4 and mAChR3 drive GAP formation in the SI and distal colon, respectively, but do not play a major role in baseline mucus secretion.
source: Thus, mAChR4 and mAChR3 drive GAP formation in the SI and distal colon, respectively, but do not play a major role in baseline mucus secretion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations with receptor antagonists.

claim: In the steady state, ACh acting on mAChR4 in the SI and mAChR3 in the distal colon triggers a response resulting in GAP formation with negligible effects on the degree of mucus secretion.
source: Our results indicate that in the steady state, ACh acting on mAChR4 in the SI and mAChR3 in the distal colon triggers a response resulting in GAP formation with negligible effects on the degree of mucus secretion (Figure 3A–H).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations shown in Figure 3A–H.

claim: Exposing intestinal explants to micro-molar concentrations of ACh induces rapid expulsion of large quantities of mucus, primarily from the intestinal crypts.
source: In contrast, exposing intestinal explants to micro-molar concentrations of ACh induces rapid expulsion of large quantities of mucus, primarily from the intestinal crypts (Ermund et al., 2013; Gustafsson et al., 2012; Phillips, 1992; Specian and Neutra, 1980).

claim: Activation of select muscarinic receptor subtypes and their respective downstream signaling pathways allows GCs to respond to ACh with either GAP formation and antigen uptake, mucus secretion, or with both processes in parallel.
source: In aggregate, these results demonstrate that activation of select muscarinic receptor subtypes and their respective downstream signaling pathways allows GCs to respond to ACh with either GAP formation and antigen uptake, mucus secretion, or with both processes in parallel.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations of differential regulation of GAP formation and mucus secretion.

claim: GAPs represent a fluid-phase endocytic pathway capable of delivering lumenal solutes across the cell by transcytosis.
source: Using high-resolution light and electron microscopy, we found that in mice, GAPs were formed by an acetylcholine (ACh)-dependent endocytic event remarkable for delivery of fluid-phase cargo retrograde into the trans-golgi network and across the cell by transcytosis – in addition to the expected transport of fluid-phase cargo by endosomes to multi-vesicular bodies and lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from high-resolution light and electron microscopy.

claim: GAP formation may have evolved as a cell-type specific and specialized endocytic pathway emerging from the basic exocytic machinery of GCs to sample and deliver luminal substances to the mucosal immune system.
source: Together these observations suggest that GAP formation may have evolved as a cell-type specific and specialized endocytic pathway emerging from the basic exocytic machinery of GCs to sample and deliver luminal substances to the mucosal immune system.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the experimental observations.

claim: GAP formation is not required to maintain the mucus barrier.
source: Our previous studies demonstrate that not all GCs form GAPs (Knoop et al., 2015; McDole et al., 2012), that GAP formation is not required to maintain the mucus barrier (Kulkarni et al., 2020), and our current findings that blockade of GAP formation does not inhibit mucus secretion, indicate that GAP formation cannot be required to maintain mucus secretion or the mucus barrier.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kulkarni et al., 2020.

claim: GAPs represent a specialized endocytic pathway enabling enhanced and regulated transcellular transport of gut lumenal solutes across the epithelial barrier by transcytosis.
source: Though compensatory endocytosis must exist following secretion in GCs, to balance membrane trafficking, the fate of these endocytic vesicles does not necessarily intersect with the GAP pathway. Rather, we suggest that GAPs represent a specialized endocytic pathway enabling enhanced and regulated transcellular transport of gut lumenal solutes across the epithelial barrier by transcytosis.
evidence: The claim is based on inference and speculation from the experimental observations.

claim: The GAP pathway likely evolved from adaptations to the secretory and membrane recovery machinery specific to this highly secretory cell type.

claim: ACh-induced GAP formation and mucus secretion are not functionally linked or dependent upon one another.
source: Despite the associations between GAP formation and mucus secretion, our results demonstrate that ACh-induced GAP formation and mucus secretion are not functionally linked or dependent upon one another.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: In spinal cord neurons, exposure to high concentrations of K+ triggers neurotransmitter release paralleled by endocytic retrieval of secretory granule membrane and uptake of high molecular weight substances from the extracellular environment.
source: In spinal cord neurons, exposure to high concentrations of K+ triggers neurotransmitter release paralleled by endocytic retrieval of secretory granule membrane and uptake of high molecular weight substances from the extracellular environment.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about spinal cord neurons.

claim: In spinal cord neurons, inhibition of K+ evoked exocytosis did not affect K+-induced endocytic retrieval of secretory granule membrane.
source: Similar to our observations demonstrating that inhibition of CCh-induced mucus secretion did not affect CCh-induced GAP formation, inhibition of K+ evoked exocytosis did not affect K+-induced endocytic retrieval of secretory granule membrane. The intact endocytic response in response to elevated K+ levels was shown to be mediated by retrieval of previously fused secretory vesicles, thus, although elevated K+ triggered secretory granule exocytosis, retrieval of previously fused granules was enough to sustain the uptake process (Neale et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Neale et al., 1999.

claim: In situations when ACh-induced mucus secretion does not occur, an intact GAP response can be maintained via retrieval of previously fused secretory granules inserted into the plasma membrane during a previous exocytotic event.
source: Applied to our data this would suggest that in situations when ACh-induced mucus secretion does not occur; an intact GAP response can be maintained via retrieval of previously fused secretory granules inserted into the plasma membrane during a previous exocytotic event.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison with spinal cord neurons.

claim: GCs secrete mucus constitutively resulting in continuous insertion of secretory granule membrane into the apical membrane to be retrieved in response to ACh.
source: In addition to secreting mucus in response to secretagogues such as ACh, GCs secrete mucus constitutively resulting in continuous insertion of secretory granule membrane into the apical membrane to be retrieved in response to ACh (Oliver and Specian, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Oliver and Specian, 1990.

claim: ACh-induced mucus secretion is initiated at the center of the GC theca.
source: Further support in favor of the two processes being functionally separate, ACh-induced mucus secretion is initiated at the center of the GC theca (Specian and Neutra, 1980), while GAPs initiate along the lateral apical surface of the cell and progress basally.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Specian and Neutra, 1980.

claim: GAPs initiate along the lateral apical surface of the cell and progress basally.

claim: The spatial separation of ACh-induced mucus secretion and GAP formation may imply that GAPs primarily form by retrieval of secretory granules released during steady state.
source: This spatial separation of the two processes may imply that GAPs primarily form by retrieval of secretory granules released during steady state, which in contrast to ACh-induced exocytosis are supplied by granules transported along the outer borders of the theca and released at the apical lateral sides (Oliver and Specian, 1990).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and inference from the spatial separation and a citation to Oliver and Specian, 1990.

source: In contrast, exposure to high concentrations of ACh was shown to increase protein release by 80%, while endocytic retrieval was increased by 40% (Gierow et al., 1995), demonstrating that, similar to what we observe in intestinal GCs, in lacrimal acinar cells, ACh-induced exocytosis and endocytosis can, at least to some degree, occur separately.

claim: In the steady state, ACh acting on mAChR4 in the SI and mAChR3 in the distal colon induces GAP formation (endocytosis) without an apparent effect on mucus secretion (exocytosis) because the intracellular Ca2+ concentration needed to trigger endocytosis is lower than that needed to trigger exocytosis.
source: This may explain why in the steady state, ACh acting on mAChR4 in the SI and mAChR3 in the distal colon induces GAP formation (endocytosis) without an apparent effect on mucus secretion (exocytosis); and yet in response to exogenous administration of high concentrations of ACh, which could trigger a larger increase in intracellular Ca2+, GCs respond with both mucus secretion and GAP formation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and the citation to Marks and McMahon, 1998.

source: In GCs, mAChR4 signaling (the pathway regulating GAP formation in the SI and proximal colon) is inhibited by activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), which in the proximal colon can occur by GC intrinsic sensing of gut microbial products via Toll-like receptors or by the presence of EGFR ligands in the SI and colon lumen (Knoop et al., 2015).

source: In summary, our results define the basis by which GCs sample lumenal antigens for delivery to the immune system and how this process is balanced with mucus secretion within the same cell.
